page: Amazon Web Services m5a.8xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features a 32 vCPU allocation backed by 16 physical cores and 32 threads running on an AMD EPYC 7571 processor clocked at 2.5 GHz. The instance is equipped with 128.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio (4.0 GB per vCPU). Networking is rated at a baseline bandwidth of 8 Gbps. There is no bundled local storage or integrated GPU hardware included with this configuration.

Benchmark data reveals distinct execution characteristics defined by its older AMD EPYC microarchitecture. Single-thread processing registers in the lowest 10% across multiple evaluations, including Geekbench single-core (725.0), single-threaded gzip compression (16.68 GB/sec), and stress-ng single-core (591.19). In contrast, multithreaded benchmarks show standard capacity, placing in the average middle 50% tier with a Geekbench multi-core score of 6369.0, PassMark CPU score of 22490.99, and stress-ng multi-core result of 9445.86. Memory bandwidth reaches 61.67 GB/sec for uncached read-only blocks and 29.63 GB/sec for write operations.

From a cost-efficiency and performance tradeoff perspective, the m5a.8xlarge provides dense parallel compute and capacity at a lower hardware tier, but lacks modern instruction sets like AVX-512 or AMX extensions. Workloads that rely on single-threaded execution speed or dense matrix mathematics will encounter bottlenecking, as evidenced by weak LLM text generation speeds on medium-sized 7B models (7.16 tokens/sec). However, it sustains stable operational throughput for multi-threaded services, reaching 19.73 million operations/sec on Redis SET benchmarks and 11.37 GB/sec in static web serving throughput.

Due to its balanced memory ratio and parallel core scaling, the m5a.8xlarge is suited for standard enterprise general-purpose workloads, distributed backend microservices, Redis caching tiers, Clang-based software build environments, and mid-sized database instances that do not require high per-core burst latency.

The instance does not bundle local disk storage or hardware GPU acceleration. Benchmark profiles indicate subdued single-core performance alongside average multi-core and memory capabilities, characterized by a PassMark CPU score of 22490.99 and Redis throughput of 19.73 million operations per second.
